canberra.title: Man dies after ute rolls, strikes tree near Goulburn
canberra.snippet: A driver has died after his ute hit a tree in the NSW Southern Tablelands. A NSW Police spokesperson said that at about 1:45 am today (31...
canberra.content:
31 July 2026

Start the conversation

Police said the driver died at the scene. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A driver has died after his ute hit a tree in the NSW Southern Tablelands.

A NSW Police spokesperson said that at about 1:45 am today (31 July), emergency services were called to Gurrundah Road at Biala, about 45 kilometres north-west of Goulburn, following reports of a crash.

On arrival, officers attached to The Hume Police District and NSW Ambulance paramedics found a Toyota Hilux had left the roadway and rolled, before crashing into a tree.

The driver, a 35-year-old man, died at the scene.

A crime scene was established and an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash commenced.

Police will prepare a report for the information of the coroner.

Anyone with information about this incident is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Information is managed on a confidential basis.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Government admits more funding needed to deliver 13,200 public housing homes by 2030
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government admits it needs additional funding to hit its target of 13,200 public homes by 2030. During Budget Estimates hearings,...
canberra.content:
Infrastructure Canberra has conceded that not every home needed to reach the target is currently funded.. Photo: ACT Government.

The ACT Government admits it needs additional funding to hit its target of 13,200 public homes by 2030.

During Budget Estimates hearings, ACT Green MLA Rebecca Vassarotti argued there appeared to be a shortfall of about 500 homes after adding together the Territory’s existing public housing stock, homes already under construction and projects funded through the new Public Housing Pipeline Program.

Catherine Loft, executive group manager at Infrastructure Canberra, did not dispute it, saying the government admits “it is an ambitious plan”.

Infrastructure Canberra admitted that not every home needed to reach the target is currently funded.

Instead, officials said the government had always planned to deliver the commitment in stages and would return to the government for additional funding before the end of the decade.

“We recognise that there is still more work to do to reach the 13,200, and we are going back to the government in two years for the funding of the remaining … to hit 13,200,” officials said.

Officials rejected suggestions this amounted to a funding gap, arguing future budgets would provide opportunities to secure the remaining investment.

“I think to say there’s a shortfall isn’t quite right because that doesn’t mean we won’t get there by the end,” the committee was told.

As of 1 July, the ACT had 12,018 public housing homes, leaving a gap of 1182 homes to meet the government’s 2030 target.

Officials told the committee 364 homes are already in various stages of planning and construction through existing programs, while the recently funded Public Housing Pipeline Program will deliver another 450 homes, including 252 already in planning and design.

The remaining homes are expected to come through future redevelopment projects, knockdown-and-rebuild programs and additional land opportunities.

The hearing also examined more than $100 million in provisional revenue attached to the new Public Housing Pipeline Program, with non-government members asking whether the funding depended on future Commonwealth contributions.

Officials said the provisional funding reflected estimates while negotiations with community housing providers continued.

“We’re not sure exactly what the details will be. We’ll need to go through a process of working with community housing providers … and there are a range of policy decisions,” officials said.

Committee members also sought assurances that homes delivered by community housing providers would ultimately be allocated to people on the public housing waiting list.

Officials said that remained the government’s expectation, although procurement and allocation arrangements were still being worked through.

Despite questions about the longer-term funding pathway, Housing ACT expressed confidence that it would meet its near-term commitments.

Officials told the committee the government’s target of renewing 1000 public housing properties and delivering 400 additional homes by June 2027 was “100 per cent achievable”.

They said 112 homes are already under construction, another 126 acquisitions are planned, and projects are being closely monitored.

“At the moment, it would come down to weather or something extraordinary,” officials said.

The questions come less than two months after housing dominated the 2026-27 ACT Budget, with the government unveiling a package worth more than $600 million to expand public and social housing.

The centrepiece was a new $364 million Public Housing Pipeline Program to build and acquire 450 public homes over the next four years, alongside funding for maintenance and renewal of existing public housing.

canberra.title: National Convention and Entertainment Centre takes major step forward
canberra.snippet: Next decade’s major infrastructure project for Canberra’s CBD has taken a step forward with the ACT Government seeking a cons...
canberra.content:
A concept image of a new National Convention Centre and Entertainment Precinct. Image: ACT Government.

Next decade’s major infrastructure project for Canberra’s CBD has taken a step forward with the ACT Government seeking a consultant to develop the business case and early design for the National Convention and Entertainment Centre to be built on the Civic pool site.

The government has released a tender for a specialist consultant team to develop a reference design for the new centre and undertake detailed planning to understand the project’s scope, costs, benefits, risks and delivery options.

It says the proposed centre is a key component of a long-term economic strategy to support the attraction of major conventions, business events, live entertainment and cultural activities to Canberra.

The project will also contribute to the ongoing transformation of the southern and eastern CBD, alongside other significant Australian and ACT governments’ investments in the precinct, such as light rail, the Canberra Aquatic Centre and the University of New South Wales (UNSW) city campus.

The project hinges on the development of a new aquatic centre in Commonwealth Park to replace the Canberra Olympic Pool.

An actual start on constructing the Convention and Entertainment Centre is not expected until the new decade.

The ACT and Albanese governments have committed $200 million in matched funding for both projects.

The Federal Government’s $100 million is being made under the National Capital Investment Framework, and includes $31.1 million for the design work and business case, to progress the Convention and Entertainment Centre Precinct project to a ‘ready for construction’ stage.

The balance of the Commonwealth’s commitment will be $68.9 million for the design and construction of the Canberra Aquatic Centre on a new site in Commonwealth Park.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr reiterated his government’s infrastructure priorities this week when announcing the new cabinet, saying the next big project after the new lyric theatre would be the Convention and Entertainment Centre.

The likely new stadium at Bruce sits behind that.

“We are making progress with the Commonwealth on the Bruce sports, health, and education precinct … so all of these projects advance but they can’t all be delivered at once for obvious reasons of both infrastructure, delivery capacity, and they need to be carefully managed from a financial perspective,” Mr Barr said.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr says the National Convention and Entertainment Centre will be the CBD’s next big project. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Announcing the tender, Mr Barr said the new National Convention and Entertainment Centre would be a once-in-a-generation infrastructure project that would help shape Canberra’s future as a growing, confident and ambitious city.

“This joint investment by the ACT and Australian governments reflects our shared commitment to delivering the infrastructure needed to support economic growth and attract major events,” he said.

“The next phase of work will ensure we have a robust business case and reference design to inform future investment decisions and position the project for delivery.”

Federal Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government Minister Catherine King said the project would transform Canberra’s city centre and support the growth of the national capital.

“This tender marks the next milestone in advancing one of Canberra’s most significant city-shaping projects under the National Capital Investment Framework,” she said.

Federal Member for Canberra Alicia Payne said the new Convention Centre would be a game changer for Canberra.

“This project will provide a significant boost to the ACT construction, tourism and hospitality sectors and has been called for by local business and tourism groups for many years,” she said.

Property Council ACT & Capital Region Executive Director Ashlee Berry said the announcement was a positive step forward for a piece of infrastructure the industry and business community had been advocating for over many years.

“A new convention and entertainment centre is critical infrastructure for a growing national capital,” she said.

“It will help Canberra attract major conferences, exhibitions, entertainment events, and business visitors, creating economic activity that flows through our hotels, restaurants, retailers and tourism operators.”

Ms Berry said Canberra’s existing convention centre had served the city well but was no longer capable of meeting the expectations of many major national and international events.

She said this was exactly the type of productivity-enhancing infrastructure Canberra needed.

Ms Berry said the Property Council looked forward to engaging constructively throughout this initial process, encouraging both levels of government to maintain momentum.

“Canberra has been talking about a new convention centre for more than a decade. This announcement is encouraging, but the community and business sector will rightly be looking for a clear pathway from planning to construction,” she said.

canberra.title: ACCI tells Treasurer to drop his ‘assault’ on small and family businesses
canberra.snippet: The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) has blasted Labor’s planned tax on discretionary trusts, describing the proposal a...
canberra.content:
ACCI Chief Executive Officer Andrew McKellar: the new policy would inflict a “massive tax increase” on small business owners. Photo. ACCI.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) has blasted Labor’s planned tax on discretionary trusts, describing the proposal as an assault on small and family businesses in Australia.

This year’s Federal Budget included a measure to require trustees of discretionary trusts to pay a minimum tax of 30 per cent on the trust’s taxable income from 1 July 2028.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says one objective of the initiative is to reduce opportunities for income splitting through discretionary trusts.

It would also more closely align the taxation of trust income with the taxation of employment income.

Testamentary trusts (estate planning tools set up inside a last will that only come into effect after death) recently secured a win, however, with genuine structures proposed to be exempt from the new tax.

The Federal Government has launched a consultation process over the planned new tax, and ACCI says Dr Chalmers should drop the whole plan.

In its submission lodged on Friday (31 July), ACCI has severely criticised the proposal, saying the new tax would raise more than $4 billion in its first year alone – at the expense of family-run businesses.

“The proposed minimum tax is not well targeted and will impose considerably higher tax and compliance costs, as well as unnecessary and excessive restructuring costs, on many family and small businesses that use discretionary trusts for legitimate commercial reasons,” the submission states.

“Discretionary trusts are a long-standing and commonly used structure for family and small businesses across Australia.

“They are regularly used in the real estate, construction, financial and professional services sectors, as well as by family businesses in retail and hospitality.

“Discretionary trusts are used because they are relatively easy to establish and simple to administer, and useful for managing commercial risk, asset protection, succession planning and variable income.”

ACCI said that if the government’s concern is tax avoidance by high-wealth individuals, it should be addressed through targeted rules and enforcement measures rather than a broad minimum tax that would capture thousands of legitimate business structures.

A discretionary trust is a legal arrangement that allows a trustee to manage assets on behalf of a group of people, which more often than not comprises family members related to a small business.

It allows business income to be shared among trust members rather than going to a single person, which is beneficial for tax purposes.

ACCI chief executive officer Andrew McKellar said the new policy would inflict a “massive tax increase” on small business owners.

“Small and family business owners across Australia have been stunned by this unprovoked assault,” Mr McKellar said.

“The government is attempting to raid the accounts of thousands of hardworking small and family businesses, despite those businesses being the backbone of the Australian economy.”

ACCI analysis shows the tax would cost small businesses alone around $4.5 billion in its first year.

The proposed 30 per cent minimum tax, paid by the trustee on trust income, is substantially higher than the average personal income tax rate currently paid by beneficiaries under existing flow-through arrangements.

The average small business trust earns about $161,000 a year.

If that income is split evenly between two beneficiaries, ACCI says, they would pay around $29,300 in total tax.

Under the government’s proposed 30 per cent minimum tax paid at the trustee level, the bill jumps to approximately $48,300.

“The government is kidding itself if it thinks this policy is designed to target high-wealth individuals. It will disproportionately hit ordinary family businesses across the country,” Mr McKellar said.

“Whether it’s your local tradie, accountant, corner store, hairdresser or family-run cafe, many of these businesses will face significantly higher tax bills under this proposal.”

In its submission, ACCI strongly urges the government to reconsider the measure.

It says the imposition of a minimum tax on trusts would penalise many small businesses at a time when they face high operating costs, business investment is weak and expected to decline further following the removal of the CGT discount, and productivity growth is anaemic.

It describes the proposal as the “opposite to a good tax policy reform”, which should ideally support small business entrepreneurship, investment and growth.

Mr McKellar said many businesses will be left with little choice but to restructure into companies to use the 25 per cent tax rate instead.

“Restructuring is not simple nor cheap and, in some cases, could exceed $50,000 in legal, accounting and financial advice fees, before any additional state stamp duties are applied on the transfer of assets from the trust to the new company,” Mr McKellar said.

“This policy will wipe out hard-earned profits at the stroke of a pen.

“The government should exempt existing small business trusts from this tax grab and allow them to continue operating under the flow-through arrangements they have relied on for decades.”

canberra.title: Former Dickson plant shop transformed into a nursery for budding artists
canberra.snippet: A former nursery building at Poppyfield Commons in Dickson will soon be transformed into an arts hub, giving Canberra creatives a new pla...
canberra.content:
Canberra artist and curator Petra Jungmanova is launching PT. Gallery, a new monthly pop-up arts space at Poppyfield Commons in Dickson. Photo: PT. Gallery.

A former nursery building at Poppyfield Commons in Dickson will soon be transformed into an arts hub, giving Canberra creatives a new place to exhibit their work, share stories and connect with the community.

The space will officially open with a soft launch on 5 August, when PT. Gallery debuts with an exhibition featuring artists from Canberra, regional NSW, Melbourne, the Blue Mountains and the United States.

Made possible through Tradies, the temporary community space at Poppyfield Commons will host the monthly pop-up gallery while the site awaits redevelopment. Curator Petra Jungmanova hopes to stage regular exhibitions there until demolition begins, with each opening combining visual art, live performances, food and storytelling.

For Jungmanova, the project is about much more than hanging artwork on walls.

“It’s about creating a place where people feel comfortable enough to stay, have a conversation and discover something they weren’t expecting,” she said.

“I wanted to create a space where art is part of everyday life, where people can bring their children, meet friends, listen to music and perhaps even speak to an artist.”

The Canberra-based artist and curator migrated to Australia from the Czech Republic after graduating from art school in 2000. She says one of the biggest cultural differences she noticed was how difficult it could be for emerging artists to find opportunities to exhibit.

“I know the pain of trying to get into a gallery, being rejected and ignored after submitting an artwork to a competition,” she said.

“Art has become a commercial commodity, and artists are being taken advantage of through ridiculous 30 and 50 per cent commissions and memberships.

“No wonder there is not much original art in people’s homes.”

That experience inspired PT. Gallery, a travelling exhibition space that gives artists, including first-time exhibitors and hobby artists, a chance to display their work without the barriers often associated with commercial galleries.

She said PT. Gallery would remain a philanthropic venture focused on giving artists, particularly emerging creatives and hobbyists, a place to exhibit without commercial barriers.

“It’s like a home away from home, so my wish for PT. Gallery visitors is to feel at home with friends kicking back,” she said.

“There is a kids’ corner with heaps of space outside, all fenced, so this venue is totally unique in its generous, cosy nature, where you can bring your kids, dogs and just hang out.”

One of Petra Jungmanova’s works celebrating Bohemian life and the rich tradition of Czech folklore and storytelling. Photo: Petra Jungmanova/PT. Gallery.

She hopes the relaxed setting will encourage people who might not normally visit an art gallery to come in, stay a while and perhaps leave having discovered a new artist.

Unlike many exhibitions, the opening show has no set theme, reflecting Jungmanova’s belief that creativity shouldn’t be confined by rules. Instead, it brings together artists from Canberra, regional NSW, Melbourne, the Blue Mountains and overseas.

Among them is Blue Mountains fine art photographer Livonne Larkins, whose dreamlike images explore moments of quiet reflection, and Florida artist Monica Foye, whose work examines the ways women have been encouraged to make themselves smaller and reclaim the space they deserve.

PT Gallery. Photo: Petra Jungmanova/PT. Gallery.

PT Gallery. Photo: Petra Jungmanova/PT. Gallery.

PT Gallery. Photo: Petra Jungmanova/PT. Gallery.

Canberra audiences will also see local photographer and illustrator Massimo Montebello’s travel photography and abstract works, paintings by Bungendore artist Kate Bender, landscapes and botanicals by Melbourne artist Cate Neal, and a posthumous collection by Czech artist Věra Červenka featuring collages, papier-mâché sculptures and decoupage.

Jungmanova will also exhibit her own paintings celebrating quiet moments of everyday family life.

The soft opening will include live line dancing, a grazing table featuring local produce and opportunities for visitors to meet the artists.

Looking ahead, PT. Gallery plans to expand beyond exhibitions, hosting storytelling evenings exploring Canberra’s history and cultural heritage, creative workshops and performances, including a classical music recital later this year.

For Jungmanova, success won’t be measured by sales.

“I just want people to walk in, feel welcome and leave having made a connection,” she said.

“In a busy world where many people don’t even know their neighbours anymore, creativity is another way communities can come together.”

PT. Gallery’s soft opening is on Wednesday, 5 August, from 5 pm to 8 pm at Poppyfield Commons. Visit Humanitix for tickets. To learn more about future pop-ups, visit Facebook.

australia.title: The rise and fall of Alan Jones, once one of Australia's most influential radio hosts  – video
australia.snippet: Born in regional Queensland in 1941 or 1943 - depending on who you ask - Alan Jones started his career as a school teacher. He ran for po...
australia.content: Born in regional Queensland in 1941 or 1943 - depending on who you ask - Alan Jones started his career as a school teacher. He ran for politics, and coached Australia's national rugby union team before becoming one of Australia’s highest-paid, most successful talkback radio presenters. 'You can't overestimate how important Alan Jones was for more than 30 years,' says Guardian Australia's Amanda Meade. Now the veteran broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two of sexual touching allegedly committed against six men between 2003 and 2020. His four-month trial begins in Sydney on Monday 3 August

australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast eSafety commissioner says court action against Teleg...
australia.content:
Icac hears of friendship breakdown between members of Reformers

Penry Buckley

Returning to the Icac’s Operation Rosny, the inquiry has heard this afternoon about how relationships between some members of the conservative right factional Liberal group the Reformers began to break down.

That includes the friendship between today’s witness, Robert Assaf, and Christian Ellis, who yesterday we heard had founded the Reformers together in 2017 after forming a strong bond while working on the No campaign for the same-sex marriage plebiscite.

Assaf said he later came to distrust Ellis, including in relation to the payment of finder’s fees to him for finding Ellis new clients.

Ellis ran Beckington, a registered lobbyist set up by the group, which allegedly took on funds under the guise of consulting services to support branch-stacking efforts, including from schools governing body Catholic Schools NSW, Beckington’s first client in 2019.

The inquiry heard that in 2021 Catholic Schools NSW CEO, Dallas McInerney, allegedly wanted to end the relationship with Beckington. Assaf said he gave the following advice to McInerney on multiple occasions in an attempt to keep payments flowing to a different company, run by Reformer Jeremy Greenwood.

He told the inquiry the advice “would have been something like”:

Christian’s a liar. He’s greedy. I don’t trust him, and I’m not sure he’s doing much for you at the moment. Jeremy seems to be picking up most of the slack. Jeremy’s starting his own company up, you may want to consider going to Jeremy.

What we learned today, Friday 31 July

That’s where we’ll leave things for the day. Thanks for reading. Here are today’s top stories:

  • The New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption Operation Rosny held another day of hearings, with evidence given that a group of young conservative Liberal power brokers accused of soliciting illegal donations used some of the funds to pay for a bucks night.

  • The London-headquartered HSBC confirmed it will close all Australian branches over the next 18 months after selling its local mortgage and personal loan portfolio to the global asset giant Blackstone.

  • Integrity expert Geoffrey Watson SC appeared before the Queensland inquiry into the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) where he defended his report into Victoria’s building industry and its allegations against underworld figure Mike Gatto.

  • David Gibson, who was discharged from the military in 1989 because he was bisexual and chair of GLBTI Rights in Ageing, said it was time for the prime minister to issue an apology to service personnel who experienced discrimination at the hands of the Australian Defence Force.

  • A funeral was held for Layla Jeffery almost a month after her body was discovered in Victorian bushland, with the teen remembered as shy but confident, and sassy but considerate.

  • A three-year investigation into one of Australia’s worst bus crashes handed down its report, finding that the 10 fatalities in the Hunter Valley in 2023 could have been reduced with better protections for ejected passengers.

  • And a Queensland driver was fined after being involved in a stunning crash in which a car became airborne and then stuck in the side of a bus in Brisbane.

Teen Layla Jeffery remembered at funeral service in rural Victoria

Layla Jeffery has been remembered at her funeral as shy but confident, sassy but considerate, almost a month after her body was discovered in bushland, AAP reports.

Jeffery, 13, was discovered dead near Donald, in Victoria’s rural west, on 9 July after she left home five days earlier.

A boy, 16, has since been charged with murder.

Mourners filed into Donald Memorial Hall for her service this afternoon.

Many wore black hoodies and Hello Kitty accessories, Layla’s favourite clothes.

Her mother, Tahlia, wore a pair of fleece-lined tartans Layla had ordered, but never got to open.

Layla’s aunt, Kaitlyn Cheyne, told mourners her niece was “something of a paradox”. She said:

She often disliked being perceived and liked to simply exist quietly alongside those she loved most.

She was both shy and confident in many different ways; funny, sassy, kind, generous, stylish, sweet, cheeky, loving and considerate.

I could go on and on and on, but it would still never be enough words to express the depth of her character, or the loss we are all feeling.

Lisa Cox

H5 bird flu detection in seagull ‘significantly widens’ geographical spread of virus, experts say

BirdLife Australia says the suspected detection of H5 bird flu in a seagull in South Australia “significantly widens the area across which the virus can be spread”.

The South Australian government said this morning state tests returned a suspected positive result for H5 bird flu in a silver gull – or seagull – found at Robe on the Limestone Coast. Samples have been sent to the CSIRO for verification.

Seagulls are one of Australia’s most common birds.

BirdLife said the development increased the risk the disease would spread into new places – including wetlands, inland or urban areas. Gulls are highly mobile, gather in large flocks, mix with other species, and are known to scavenge on carcasses.

BirdLife national affairs adviser Sean Dooley said:

The reason silver gulls elevate our concern is that they move around far more widely than greater crested terns.

That broadens the area across which the virus could appear next.

He said governments and communities would need to be extra vigilant in more places and “targeted surveillance will need to broaden beyond the coastline”.

What we’re seeing now suggests very strongly that we’re at the beginning of a long and difficult fight against a virus that has decimated wildlife populations overseas.

Victorian teachers vote to strike for third time this year in pay dispute

Victorian teachers will walk off the job for a third time in five months after negotiations stalled in their bitter pay and conditions dispute with the state government, AAP reports.

Earlier today, the Australian Education Union announced a 24-hour stop work action in Victorian state schools on 19 August after an internal meeting.

Unless the parties can come to an agreement, it will be the state’s third major teachers’ strike this year.

The most recent strike took place on 23 July, with school gates locked across Victoria as 20,000 educators descended on Melbourne’s CBD to demand better pay and working conditions.

The statewide strike took place a week after Victorian union members narrowly rejected a revised government pay offer.

The deal, which was opposed by 51.8%, would have increased pay for teachers and support staff by at least 28.3% over four years, with an increase of 12.75% by October this year.

The newly minted Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, who served as education minister under former leader Jacinta Allan, argued the latest rejected pitch was a “watershed moment for education” that would have made Victorian teachers the best paid in Australia.

The president of the Victorian branch of the teachers’ union, Justin Mullaly, said negotiations with the government had not progressed since the last pay offer was put on the table on 17 July.

Mullaly acknowledged the latest pay offer was “significant”, but said it was not enough to meet the needs of overworked, underpaid educators.

He said:

Only three-in-10 teachers are saying they’ll stick around until retirement.

That’s no good for our public education, that’s no good for our children and young people that we teach.

Penry Buckley

Sloane has previously declined to provide running commentary on Icac’s hearings after other current shadow ministers were named during hearings, but Rath’s admission relates to conduct prior to the current inquiry.

In a statement today, she said:

I have spoken with Chris directly. I have expressed my disappointment about what occurred and made it clear to him the standards I expect of every member of my team. Those standards are high, and I expect them to be upheld at all times.

I respect the Parliament’s processes. It is not appropriate for me to simply substitute my own judgment years later for the findings and sanctions imposed by the Parliament after it had considered all the facts.

NSW opposition leader backs minister linked to Reformers

Penry Buckley

The NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, has backed in a minister who has been linked to the conservative rightwing factional group called the Reformers, which is being investigated under Icac’s Operation Rosny.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported today that NSW Liberal shadow planning minister, Chris Rath, had been captured by wire tap helping members of the Reformers evade summons to appear before a 2023 parliamentary inquiry which preceded the Icac’s Operation Rosny inquiry.

In a statement, Rath, who later recused himself from the committee, said he was “apologetic” for the incident, which had been dealt with by the NSW Privileges Committee, which had issued him a caution.

Rath said in the statement:

This Inquiry commenced in the highly politically charged context of an election campaign, and at the time I didn’t comprehend the gravity of the allegations.

As resolved by the Labor majority Privileges Committee, the Clerk reminded me of my obligations, and I was, and am, apologetic. No further action was taken.

I am not under investigation by ICAC, nor have I been called as a witness to the inquiry or asked to provide any evidence.

Catie McLeod

Hi, I hope you’re having a nice Friday. I’ll take it from here.

Nick Visser

That’s it for me. Catie McLeod will pick up the blog from here. Take care!

Safety failings compounded deadly wedding bus crash

Fatalities in one of Australia’s worst bus crashes could have been reduced with better protections for ejected passengers, a three-year investigation has found.

AAP reports 10 mostly young wedding guests were killed in a bus tip-over at a roundabout in Greta in the NSW Hunter Valley in 2023, with a further 25 injured.

Driver Brett Andrew Button, 60, received a decades-long prison sentence for his role in the crash, as he was under the influence of an opioid painkiller and driving too fast at the time.

The Office of Transport Safety Investigations on Friday handed down an investigation report into the crash. Chief investigator Jim Modrouvanos said Button should not have been behind the wheel on the night of the crash, but added passenger protection systems had not worked effectively.

He said not all passengers wore seatbelts fitted in the coach and they were not issued with a pre-trip safety warning as was company policy.

Modrouvanos delivered 41 recommendations in total, and government regulators, operators and organisations have accepted wholly or in principle the 34 recommendations relevant to them.

They included strengthening medication management, developing a centralised driver performance system, increasing seatbelt management and a review of minimum rollover-protection requirements.

Trial for mother and daughter over alleged Islamic State ties

Two accused women with links to Islamic State have been committed to stand trial as their cases are fast-tracked to the supreme court, AAP reports.

Kawsar Ahmad, 54, and her daughter Zeinab Ahmad, 31, appeared in Melbourne magistrates court via video link on Friday as they entered their “not guilty” pleas.

The two women were charged with slavery offences in May after returning to Australia with other family members of former Islamic State fighters.

It’s alleged Kawsar migrated to the Middle Eastern country to join IS with her husband, Mohammed, Zeinab and their other children about January 2015. It’s alleged while in Syria in 2017, Mohammed bought a teenage girl as a slave for $US10,000.

The two women each made a bid for bail in June but only Kawsar was successful, with a magistrate finding she posed a very low risk to the community. Kawsar’s bail was extended to her supreme court date, with conditions including a prohibition from attending any mosques to continue.

Zeinab was refused bail because there was no compelling evidence she had renounced the terrorist group. She was remanded in custody after not making any further bail applications.

Penry Buckley

Icac witness describes being ‘hangry’ before lunchtime break

The NSW Icac’s hearings have resumed after a break for lunch. Just before lunch, the Icac presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, who has frequently intervened during Reformer Robert Assaf’s evidence today, told Assaf he had become “a bit argumentative in your response”.

“I believe they call that hangry commissioner,” Assaf said.

Gleeson said:

I’m not aware of what young people’s speak is these days, Mr Assaf. What I’d like you to do is to sit there, concentrate and answer a further question which council assisting has, and then we’ll adjourn. Understand?

The commission heard how Assaf, 30, came to be employed in communications at Catholic Schools NSW, the governing body for 600 schools in the state, in 2019, alongside Reformers associate Dylan Whitelaw, who gave evidence earlier in the week.

The Catholic Schools NSW chief executive, Dallas McInerney, is alleged to have arranged and approved payments to the Reformers to support branch stacking efforts through registered lobbyist Beckington, where Whitelaw later came to be employed.

Under intense questioning before lunch from counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, Assaf admitted that he knew that money being paid to Beckington was to fund work that Whitelaw was doing for the Reformers. “I knew that, yes,” Assaf said.

Australia’s golden sprinters speak out on cycling defector: ‘Good riddance’

Leigh Hoffman has bade Matt Richardson good riddance after Australia’s gold medal in the team sprint on day one of the Commonwealth Games track cycling program, AAP reports.

Teammate Ryan Elliott also joked they had cleared Hoffman as their leader, checking his passport to make sure he will stay in the Australian program. While expressing sympathy for Richardson after a recent nasty race crash in Japan, his former teammates finally spoke freely about the shock defection.

Their big win over England was one of Australia’s three cycling gold medals at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, along with the women’s team pursuit and para-cyclist Tara Neyland.

But England gained some revenge for the Paris Olympics, beating Australia in the men’s team pursuit final. Two years ago, Australia narrowly downed Great Britain in a pulsating ride-off for gold. Soon after Paris, Richardson stunned the sport by switching allegiances to Great Britain.

Read more here:

Ima Caldwell

Toyota becomes airborne and then wedges in side of Brisbane bus

A Queensland driver has been fined after being involved in a stunning crash that saw a car become airborne and then stuck in the side of a bus.

The drama unfolded at Rocklea in Brisbane’s south on Wednesday evening. A blue Toyota Yaris hit a traffic island and was catapulted into the air before smashing into the side of the council bus. The back of the car was left protruding from the bus.

australia.title: ‘Rob has the bucks cash’: NSW Liberals used Reformers funds to pay for ‘personal expenditure’, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Robert Assaf separately tells anti-corruption inquiry money funnelled through lobbying firm to create ‘maximum benefit from a tax perspec...
australia.content:
A group of young conservative Liberal power brokers accused of soliciting illegal donations used some of the funds to pay for a bucks night, one of its members has told a corruption inquiry.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday heard again from Robert Assaf, who this week was the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.

The inquiry is investigating allegations that the Reformers solicited or accepted illegal donations to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch stacking”. The group wanted more conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.

The counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asked Assaf about a decision to move alleged payments from prohibited donor Michael O’Hara from a bank account in the Reformers’ name to Beckington, a registered lobbying firm set up by the group and run by member Christian Ellis.

O’Hara earlier this week admitted to a fake arrangement in which he paid Beckington for “strategic wealth strategy investment advice”. He disputed whether the payments to the Reformers were to the NSW Liberals or should be considered political donations.

On Friday, Assaf said funnelling money through Beckington rather than the Reformers account was to create “the maximum benefit from a tax perspective”.

Dwyer replied: “That’s an explanation that you thought of overnight. Is that right?”

Asked if he was aware that it was illegal to minimise tax by creating fake invoices, Assaf said he knew that now, but not at the time. Asked if he thought the arrangement was “dishonest”, he said: “I would have thought it was tricky.”

Assaf admitted to temporarily using funds from the Reformers account to pay for a bucks night.

In a WhatsApp message to the group in August 2020, Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet, the brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet, wrote: “Rob has the bucks cash coming back.”

Asked what this meant, Assaf said: “I think you recall I referred to us being immature and young, using the account as an advance on our personal expenditure.”

“This was one of those moments where we, I think, we had booked a venue for either my bucks or Christian [Ellis’s] bucks. It required an upfront payment,” he said.

“I think it was cancelled, maybe because of Covid, one of them, so it was waiting for it to get reimbursed.”

Assaf said he had issued fake invoices to Beckington in the name of his wife, Carmel Assaf, but did not agree that this was to reimburse him for Reformers work. He said he had done so to claim a 10% fee promised to him for finding new clients for Ellis.

The commission heard Assaf was employed in communications at Catholic Schools NSW, the governing body for 600 schools in the state, in 2019, alongside Reformers associate Dylan Whitelaw, who gave evidence earlier in the week.

The Catholic Schools NSW chief executive, Dallas McInerney, is alleged to have arranged and approved payments to the group to support branch stacking efforts through Beckington, where Whitelaw later came to be employed.

Assaf disputed an earlier claim made by Whitelaw that he spent 60% of his time at Catholic Schools NSW on factional work, saying it was more like 10 to 20%. But he said he would sometimes “chuck a sickie” to do Reformers work.

Under questioning from Dwyer, Assaf admitted that he knew that money being paid to Beckington was to fund work that Whitelaw was doing for the Reformers. “I knew that, yes,” Assaf told the hearing.

The inquiry heard that Assaf’s friendship with Ellis later broke down.

The inquiry heard that when McInerney allegedly wanted to end the relationship with Beckington in 2021, Assaf provided the former with advice about it on “multiple” occasions.

“[That advice] would have been something like: ‘Christian’s a liar. He’s greedy. I don’t trust him, and I’m not sure he’s doing much for you at the moment,” he said.

The inquiry on Friday returned to whether the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, had knowledge of and supported the Reformers.

Assaf said he recalled sending a screenshot of a message from McInerney in which he said he wanted to “shake down Angus for 10K”, and reading a message sent by Whitelaw in which he claimed McInerney had received “the commitment from Angus, the 15k injection plus a 3k monthly donation”, but denied any donation had taken place.

“I don’t think Angus worked out,” Assaf said. Taylor, who is not accused of wrongdoing, on Friday again denied making payments to the group.

The Icac presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened on multiple occasions during Assaf’s evidence. Before the lunch break, Gleeson told Assaf he had become “a bit argumentative in your response”.

“I believe they call that hangry commissioner,” Assaf said.

Gleeson said: “I’m not aware of what young people’s speak is these days, Mr Assaf. What I’d like you to do is to sit there, concentrate, and answer a further question which council assisting has, and then we’ll adjourn. Understand?”

Assaf was expected to appear again on Monday, before the commission is scheduled to hear from the NSW shadow attorney general and Liberal leader in the upper house, Damien Tudehope.

Many of the Reformers worked as staffers in Tudehope’s office, and Tudehope gave frequent talks at Reformers recruitment events. O’Hara is his former business partner.

Tudehope, who has stood aside from his shadow cabinet roles during the inquiry, is not accused of wrongdoing.

The inquiry will also hear from Jean-Claude Perrottet and Jeremy Greenwood, both named in Icac’s allegations. The watchdog heard on Thursday that Jean-Claude Perrottet allegedly paid for memberships as part of branch-stacking efforts, forbidden under Liberal party rules.

He has previously denied any wrongdoing, while Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing.

Icac’s hearings continue.

australia.title: Gina Rinehart threatens ABC with legal action over Race Around the World program
australia.snippet: Hancock Prospecting says chair Kim Williams among those ‘on notice’ for failing to remove program that joked about turning Rinehart’s ins...
australia.content:
Gina Rinehart has threatened the ABC with legal action over crude comments aired on the national broadcaster, including a joke about mixing her guts into a sausage roll.

The four-minute film, titled A Very Relaxing Video, aired on the Race Around the World program on 12 July and concluded with the film-maker, Kate McGuinness, making crude and offensive comments about Rinehart.

“When the revolution comes will you hide under the bed or will you know exactly how to shove a stick right up Gina Rinehart’s butthole, stirring it round, mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll to make something out of nothing?” she said.

On Friday, Hancock Prospecting released a statement detailing that it first wrote to the ABC board on 23 July. The company said the ABC was asked to “immediately remove” the segment from all of its platforms; publicly apologise to Rinehart; and “undertake a comprehensive investigation” into how it was approved and published.

“One week has now elapsed,” the statement said.

“The ABC’s Board and senior management have provided no substantive public response, nor any substantive response to Hancock or Mrs Rinehart, and have taken no steps to remove the material from ABC platforms, despite widespread public condemnation and the serious risks its publication and continued publication pose to Mrs Rinehart.”

According to Hancock, it has sent legal letters to the ABC’s chair, Kim Williams; deputy chair, Lisa Caffery; and its managing director, Hugh Marks.

It said the letter informed them they have been formally placed on notice over “detailed allegations of serious contraventions of multiple Australian criminal and civil laws arising from the ABC’s publication and continued publication of the material”.

News24 first reported that the mining magnate had “launched legal action” against the ABC and several senior executives.

On Friday, the ABC on Friday confirmed it had received the legal letters.

“The ABC has received correspondence from lawyers acting for Ms Rinehart and will respond to it in due course,” a spokesperson said. “The ABC Ombudsman is independently reviewing audience complaints in relation to the 12 July Race Around the World episode in accordance with the ABC’s complaints handling process.”

The episode, which was rated M for “coarse language” and “sexual references”, was still available to stream on iView on Friday afternoon.

On Thursday, McGuinness issued an apology and said it wasn’t her intention to promote violence.

“My writing is cartoonish and always satirical. Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally,” she said in a statement uploaded to the ABC’s website.

Pressure had been mounting on the ABC to respond amid wide outrage in sectors of the media and from the Western Australian premier, Roger Cook, who said the skit was “unacceptable” and used “confronting” language.

The media regulator said it would wait until the results of the ABC’s processes before making a decision on any next steps.

“Under Australia’s co-regulatory broadcasting system set out in the Broadcasting Services Act … national broadcasters are given the first opportunity to respond to complaints about alleged breaches of their respective codes of practice,” a spokesperson for the Australian Communications and Media Authority (Acma) said.

“If complainants are dissatisfied with the broadcaster’s response or do not receive a response within the statutory timeframe, complainants may make their complaint to the Acma.”

world.title: At least 41 people die as thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident Europe live – latest upda...
world.content:
At least 41 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in a matter of hours, triggering a political crisis for the Madrid government and unleashing a barrage of criticism from other EU countries.

The large influx of people arriving in Ceuta by swimming across from neighbouring Morocco or scaling the border fence has caught the city of 85,000 off guard and resulted in what one local police association called a “serious humanitarian crisis”.

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday, described the influx as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity” and said he would use all the state resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the people of Ceuta.

He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules.

Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.”

Sánchez, who is under pressure from political opponents and other European countries to come up with a swift and comprehensive response, said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain.

He also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, to legally comply with the court’s ruling.

Spain’s interior ministry said about 25,000 people had voluntarily crossed the border back into Morocco during the course of Friday.

The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when 10,000 people entered the territory over the course of two days by taking advantage of a loosening of border controls by Morocco.

That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.

That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group.

Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.

Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations”, and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.

On Thursday evening, Spain’s interior ministry announced that 60 members of the armed forces would be deployed to Ceuta, along with an additional 30 Guardia Civil officers. “The armed forces will reinforce the Guardia Civil in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain security in the city of Ceuta,” the ministry said.

But the situation is evolving rapidly as the city struggles to cope with the massive number of arrivals.

Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing Guardia Civil officers, described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”. He said: “People are still entering. The reinforcements that have arrived are only helping the injured and other humanitarian efforts.”

Without shelter, thousands of people including unaccompanied children had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly, Sbihi said. “It’s chaotic,” he added.

Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said.

Video footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children.

“Viva España!” some shouted to a freelance photographer working for the Associated Press. It was not immediately clear what had prompted so many people to cross to Ceuta.

Ceuta and Melilla have the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reach Europe.

Juan Jesús Vivas, the mayor-president of Ceuta, demanded the deployment of additional police and troops “to guarantee the inviolability of the frontier” and citizens’ safety. He also called on the central government to declare a national emergency over the crossings.

But the government rejected calls for the declaration of a national emergency, saying such emergencies could not be declared over migration issues, and could be declared only in response to dire meteorological events – such as the current wildfires – or in the face of a volcanic or nuclear threat.

Events in Ceuta have led some other EU countries to issue threats or rebukes.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

Meloni said Italy was prepared to take “extraordinary measures” to defend its borders, claiming that the “shocking” scenes from Ceuta demonstrated that “illegal immigration poses a real threat to the security of Europe’s borders”.

Meloni, whose government has been struggling to regain traction since it lost a referendum in March on an overhaul of the judiciary, appears to be exploiting the incident for political gain before general elections next year in which she faces competition from a new hard-right rival, Roberto Vannacci. She has made security her key political offering.

Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now-closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.

Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”.

The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said he had given instructions for the strengthening of controls at the Spanish border.

The former French prime minister Michel Barnier was more outspoken, saying France “cannot suffer the consequences of its neighbours’ migration choices”. He also appeared to criticise Spain’s regularisation scheme, saying: “If a member state makes decisions that create a pull factor for migration, we must be able to immediately protect our borders … Mastering immigration is a condition of sovereignty, security and trust between European states.”

The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”.

The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen, said that as “Spain has completely failed to protect the Schengen Area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status.

In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) has called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the small military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient.

In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.”

The far-right Vox party, meanwhile, called the incident “an invasion”.

world.title: Archbishop of Canterbury vows to support £100m pledge helping communities affected by enslavement
world.snippet: During her first visit to Ghana, Dame Sarah Mullally expressed regret and said the controversial fund symbolises the Christian belief in ...
world.content:
At a former British castle where thousands of enslaved Africans were held before being shipped across the Atlantic, the archbishop of Canterbury expressed “lament” for the Church of England’s involvement in transatlantic chattel slavery and reaffirmed her commitment to a controversial £100m fund for affected communities.

Dame Sarah Mullally made the comments on Thursday during a visit to the Cape Coast castle, a 17th-century fortress that was built by Swedish traders, but occupied by the Danish and the Dutch, before the British seized it in 1664.

It was part of a 10-day tour of Ghana and Cameroon at the invitation of the head of the Anglican church’s west Africa province, the Archbishop Cyril Kobina Ben-Smith. Both countries are part of the church’s west Africa province.

“Being at Cape Coast Castle today and seeing the horrific conditions that thousands of people were kept in, it is impossible not to feel the weight of the immense evil that drove the transatlantic slave trade,” the archbishop said at the site.

She was shown the dungeons used to keep enslaved people, before praying in a former Anglican chapel above them. She also visited the “Door of No Return”, where enslaved people were loaded on to ships and ferried across the Atlantic.

Her trip began in Accra, 142km east of Cape Coast on Sunday. There in the capital, Mullally visited four local parishes and delivered the sermon at a special Eucharistic service at St Joseph the Worker Anglican church in the Kaneshie area. According to local reports, the service was officiated by an all-female clergy from the Anglican church of Ghana.

Mullally, who in March became the 106th head of the 492-year-old denomination and the only woman to do so, also met the Ghanaian president, John Mahama, earlier in the tour, along with her husband, Eamonn Mullally.

Since the government launched the Year of Return scheme in 2019 to help Africans and their descendants in the diaspora reconnect with their roots, Ghana has had a surge in visitors. As part of Mullally’s visit, she laid a foundation stone for a hostel belonging to the local church’s culture resort initiative, to accommodate pilgrims from the diaspora wanting to engage in the scheme.

The archbishop also preached at a service of more than 1,000 nurses in the town of Mampong, where she commissioned a new campus clinic named after her. On Friday, she heads to Yaoundé, the Cameroonian capital and will then proceed to Douala and the English-speaking cities of Buea and Limbe.

Ghana has been spearheading a global campaign to seek reparative justice and last month hosted a landmark conference attended by heads of state from more than 80 countries.

The archbishop’s visit comes three years after her predecessor Justin Welby formally apologised for the church’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, including using a fund for poor clergy to invest in enslaving Africans. “It is a stain on the wider church that some Christians did not see their brothers and sisters as created in the image of God, but as objects to be exploited,” he said.

The church set up a £100m fund committed to “a programme of investment, research and engagement” in communities affected by slavery, triggering diverse reactions. At the time, an independent oversight group argued that the amount was insufficient to address the generational damage slavery had caused and urged the church to expand that commitment to £1bn. Upon Mullally’s ascension to the role of archbishop, a committee of Conservative MPs urged her to spend the money on wages for the church’s clergy.

However, on Thursday, the archbishop reaffirmed her commitment tothe fund. “We played a part in the transatlantic slave trade … part of the Christian belief in repentance is about action, so we are putting in place action to support those communities that feel the legacy of the slave trade,” she said.

Across Ghana, the mood has largely been celebratory. On a visit to the palace of the Asantehene, the traditional ruler of the Asante people in the city of Kumasi on Wednesday, Mullally wore a special cassock and cape lined with kente cloth that excited palace chiefs.

Among those who were not enthused was Accra-based accountant Kenneth Mordzro, who believes the church can play a greater role in reparation efforts. “They should bring back the gold and artefacts they stole from our ancestors during the colonial days,” he said, referring to loot taken by the British government during the Anglo-Asante wars of the 19th century.

world.title: Ebola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virus
world.snippet: As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers f...
world.content:
The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus.

At 3,360 confirmed cases, the disease is now affecting people in five provinces in the east of the DRC, with 1,487 deaths recorded, representing an overall case fatality rate estimated at about 45%, according to Congolese health officials. Health responses to the outbreak have been badly hampered by conflict in many of the affected areas.

“I fear that at some point, life may come to a standstill here in our province of Ituri,” said Deborah Nzuva, a mother of four who lives in Rwampara, one of the affected regions. “We were already in a precarious situation before the Ebola virus disease, which continues to claim its victims.”

Since officially declared by the Congolese authorities on 15 May, the Bundibugyo strain of the virus has spread faster than any of the country’s 16 previous Ebola outbreaks – and the numbers are approaching the previous worst toll, in 2018-2020 when 3,470 people in DRC were infected.

Prof Pierre Akilimali, from the country’s public health institute (NPHI), is in charge of the Ebola response. He emphasises that the disease continues to spread and that it is still difficult to know when it will reach its peak. According to him, there is a way to go and the road to bringing the outbreak under control is a long one.

“Here in Ituri, we have the issues of insecurity, mining and high population density, which make the current outbreak more complex than previous ones,” he said.

The Congolese authorities say they have taken a number of measures to limit spread, including strengthening surveillance through community liaison officers, building more than 20 Ebola treatment centres, and setting up local laboratories for testing. “The public must also play their part by seeking medical advice at the slightest suspicion of infection,” Akilimali said. “This will help us to respond effectively to the disease.”

He said cases continue to rise in the Bunia and Rwampara health zones, with between 100 and 150 new confirmed infections each week.

Annabelle Nissi, a clothing trader in Bunia, said people were living in fear.

“This outbreak is causing us great distress. Our hope lies solely in God’s hands. It continues to disrupt our lives and has brought our development projects to a standstill,” she said.

Dr Justus Nsio, field incident manager for the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said it was a race against time.

“All the experts monitoring this outbreak agree that it was detected too late. When detection is delayed, we have to work hard to make up for what we missed earlier in order to contain the disease,” he said.

“What is certain is that, with the commitment of the movement and our partners, the outcome will be favourable.”

Clinical trials began in early July of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no standard treatment.

As of 15 July, about 20 people had been enrolled in these trials, which could last up to four months, according to Prof Placide Mbala, head of laboratory operations for the Ebola response in the DRC.

Uganda, which this week declared the Ebola outbreak over on its territory, 12 days after its last case was reported, has sent experts to the DRC to work alongside their Congolese counterparts, particularly in the border regions of Tchomia and Kasenyi.

world.title: US government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conference
world.snippet: State department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in Brazil A US government ma...
world.content:
A US government map of Africa mislabeled every country during a state department presentation at a ⁠global conference in Brazil ⁠this week, ​causing a stir among attenders who took screenshots and posted them online.

Reuters viewed a video of the presentation given at the Aids 2026 conference in ⁠Rio de Janeiro, which shows the errant map displayed halfway during a presentation about the state department’s new health agreements.

A Reuters analysis found the image of the map included ⁠in the presentation contained an artificial intelligence watermark that signals it was made with OpenAI tools. The ​company said it was investigating the report.

The state ‌department said it took “full responsibility” ‌for the confusion caused and that the map had been produced by a team member who hastily changed ‌the slide deck before the event.

The map showed Nigeria, where the US currently has several hundred troops deployed, as landlocked in the Sahara desert. Mozambique, which is in south-eastern Africa, was relocated to the Horn of Africa, while Côte d’Ivoire in west Africa was placed on the other side of the continent.

Screenshots of the map first appeared in a Substack post by the Aids expert Emily Bass and were widely ‌shared on LinkedIn, with one post garnering about 40,000 views.

“Whoever created and approved this slide did not know where countries in Africa are and did not care to ​check their work,” wrote Matt Petit, who focuses on AI and geopolitics at the Atlantic Council, in the post.

In a statement, the state department said: “We take full responsibility for the confusion and misrepresentation it caused for attendees, including our African partners.” The speaker at the conference was Jeff Graham, the ⁠top US health envoy who oversees the initiative known as the President’s Emergency Plan ​for Aids Relief, or Pepfar. He ​did not reply to requests for comment.

The ​state department said the discussions at the conference were “substantive and constructive” despite the map ​and that it remained ‌committed to fighting Aids ​with real results. The ​Trump administration’s decision last year to pause funding pending a review disrupted aid programs worldwide, but Pepfar’s core work such as the provision of life-saving drugs has largely resumed. The US is scaling back other areas of its spending including on prevention and surveillance, and plans to fully phase out the program in South Africa.

world.title: Fifteen elephant deaths in Kenya may be due to cyanide poisoning
world.snippet: Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service The recent deaths of 15...
world.content:
The recent deaths of 15 elephants near a park in southern Kenya were likely caused by the animals ingesting pesticides used on tomato farms, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) has said.

Erustus Kanga, the agency’s director general, told Citizen TV that analysis of samples collected from the carcasses had found traces of cyanide, a chemical compound used in farming as a predator control poison and a pest fumigant, which has also been used by poachers.

“Cyanide is a highly toxic chemical,” he said. “If elephants consume cyanide, they cannot survive a day or two.”

The deaths occurred in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku Group ranch areas around Amboseli national park, an area covering 392 sq km (96,865 acres) and that, together with other neighbouring conservancies are home to more than 1,600 elephants.

Kimana town is a leading tomato producer and a place where researchers at the Route to Food Initiative, a food rights programme, have previously reported the use of a cyanide substance on the crop.

Isaac Lekolool, the head of veterinary and capture services at KWS, told Citizen TV that the stomach contents of one member of a herd that roamed Kimana sanctuary included “lots of tomatoes,” suggesting agrochemical poisoning.

Kanga warned that the effects could reach a wider population, as livestock may also eat from farms in the area.

“We have the goats, we have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this cyanide is truly the one that is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact.”

On Tuesday, KWS announced it was investigating the deaths of the elephants from 24 June and 24 July in Amboseli. It said 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and that preliminary tests had detected a potential toxic substance.

Benson Leyian, the CEO of Big Life Foundation, a conservation organisation that operates in the area surrounding Amboseli national park, said the elephant deaths were a cause for concern.

“Thanks to decades of community-centred conservation, the Amboseli elephant population is one of the best protected in Africa, and elephant poaching has been virtually eliminated here. Aside from losses during periods of severe drought, we haven’t seen a cluster of elephant deaths like this for some time,” he said.

In a statement, the International Fund for Animal Welfare described the deaths as “deeply alarming”, adding the incident “reinforces why we must continue investing in science, monitoring, and collaborative conservation efforts”.

“Every elephant lost is significant – not only for the species, but for the health of the ecosystems they help sustain and the communities that live alongside them,” it said.

Farmers and herders in Kenya have in the past poisoned wildlife in retaliation for eating their crops and livestock.

In Zimbabwe, poachers have killed dozens of elephants by lacing watering holes and salt licks with the chemical compound.

The Amboseli ecosystem is a major source of tourism revenue, but tensions have been building in recent months as local leaders demand the handover of the park’s management and operations to the government of Kajiado county, where it is located. Earlier this month, a court suspended the county government’s takeover.
